chunks: If you conclude an agreement between yourself and your enemy, or grant him a pledge of security from you,
then fulfill your covenant with fidelity, and guard your pledge with trustworthiness, and make yourself a shield against whatever you have given [in guarantee],
for there is no obligation of Allah that people are more united upon, despite the divergence of their desires and the scattering of their opinions, than the honoring of fulfilling covenants,
and indeed the polytheists adhered to that among themselves even more than the Muslims, because they experienced the consequences of treachery,
so do not deceive in your pledge, nor cheat in your covenant, nor trick your enemy, for he who is bold against Allah is only an ignorant, wretched one.
ai.seo_question: What are the key ethical principles for a governor regarding treaties and trustworthiness according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this foundational directive from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) establishes covenant-keeping (al-wafa’ bi-l-‘ahd) as a supreme ethical pillar, transcending sectarian divides by noting that even polytheists honored treaties to avoid the fallout of treachery. He frames the governor’s self as a shield protecting the integrity of these agreements, warning that breaking trust is a mark of the 'wretched ignorant' who dare defy divine expectation. This instruction underscores the political theology of justice, where internal consistency in governance reflects broader spiritual accountability.
